comment: Checks design-flow can run against a USER'S repo. Format documented in rails-flow/checks.json.
rendered_conformance.py is deliberately absent: it needs a browser, which is the user's
dependency. A gate that skips when Playwright is missing reads as a pass, so it stays in the
agent-driven browser pass where its absence is visible.
brand-pack was broken from the day it was written and nothing here could have caught it: it
named `app/assets/stylesheets/brand`, a path /design-flow:setup never creates (packs live in
`brands/<slug>/`), so it was permanently NOT APPLICABLE -- and it passed no pack directory, so
on the one repo where it did apply it would have exited 2 on a usage error. Not-applicable is
not a pass, which is exactly why project_gates.py says so on every run.

checks.why: The component mandate was prose, and prose drifts where nothing checks it. Measured on a consumer app: ZERO raw form fields, where a request spec asserted anatomy; EIGHTEEN raw buttons, where only a sentence did. Nine retyped the class string and one copy appeared three times, omitting a class the component had gained because a table action column broke mid-word -- carrying the exact defect the component was fixed for, unable to receive the fix. The second rule is the cause of the first: a component that cannot take a caller's data- or form- attribute is one a developer writes by hand instead.
Variants that differ in anything but composition are a fork of the design system, and a switcher route left reachable in production ships every rejected screen.
A pack moves upstream and the project stands still — drift enters with NO local edit, so no change-triggered mechanism can catch it. Only an unconditional check can.

A port that implements three of an artboard's seven sections passes the design-system audit and can say it is done; the manifest extracted from the canvas is the denominator, and the port report must account for every item by id, with implemented text found where it says.
